notes.meaning: Six Levites are named who had married foreign women. Levites were temple assistants who helped the priests with worship and daily duties, so their compromise was especially dangerous. By listing them, Ezra showed that even sacred workers were held to God's standard.

One temple singer and three gatekeepers are listed among those who had taken foreign wives. The gatekeepers guarded the temple doors, and the singers led worship songs to God. Their public roles meant their repentance had to be open and complete as well.

The list shifts to the ordinary Israelites, starting with seven men from the family of Parosh. These were regular citizens rather than priests or Levites. God expects every believer, not just religious leaders, to obey His word.

Six men from the family of Elam had also married foreign women. Shechaniah, the man who first urged Ezra to lead this reform, belonged to this very clan. He showed true courage by supporting God's law even when his own relatives were guilty.

Six men from the clan of Zattu are recorded here as having foreign wives. This family had returned from exile in Babylon to help restore God's people in the land. Rebuilding the community meant setting aside sinful practices picked up from surrounding nations.

Four men from the family of Bebai are named in the public record. They had broken God's law by marrying outside the covenant community. Setting their homes in order was a painful but necessary step toward renewal.

Six men from the family of Bani are listed among the offenders. They openly admitted their wrongdoing and agreed to correct it before the assembly. True repentance requires being honest about our faults instead of concealing them.

Eight men from the family of Pahath-moab are listed here. Pahath-moab was one of the largest and most influential clans among the returned exiles. Prominence and high family standing did not excuse anyone from the Lord's commands.

Eight men from the clan of Harim are recorded as having taken foreign wives. They agreed to separate from their unlawful marriages to keep Israel faithful to the Lord. God calls His people to honor their covenant with Him above every other loyalty.

Seven men from the family of Hashum were found to have married foreign women. They joined the rest of the people in turning away from this disobedience. God offers forgiveness and a fresh start when sinners turn from their wrong choices.

Nine men from another family branch of Bani are named across these lines. Their inclusion shows how thoroughly the committee investigated each household. God cares about thorough obedience in every part of life.

Three more men from this same family clan are recorded. They also agreed to send away the foreign wives they had taken. Even small groups of offenders had to be dealt with to restore holiness to the people.
Four men from the family of Binnui are listed here. They were part of the group of returnees working to follow God's law. Spiritual health for the whole nation depended on integrity in every family.

Three more men from the family of Binnui are named. In some ancient copies, the first name is written as Mabnadebai instead of Machnadebai. The Lord takes notice of each individual person, both in their failures and in their repentance.

Another three men from this family line appear in the record of those who took foreign wives. Recording each name ensured that the community held everyone to their pledge. Real spiritual growth requires full honesty about past sins.

Three final men from the family of Binnui complete this branch's list. Together, eighty-six ordinary laymen from ten different families were identified during the inquiry. The community showed great care in dealing with every case without favoritism.

Seven men from the descendants of Nebo are listed, ending the roster of ordinary Israelites. Nebo was an ancestral family or town from the return from Babylon. This final family group shows that no household was overlooked in the reform.

About one hundred and thirteen men in all had taken foreign wives, and some of them had children with them. Having children made sending the wives away far more painful and difficult, showing how strictly the reform was carried out. Some older commentators believed that having few children was God's mercy to ease the separation, while others suggest the children stayed to be raised in the true faith.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars note that the Hebrew text at the end of the verse is grammatically difficult, and some ancient versions suggest the wives and children were sent away together.
